idiom_name: `Builder method(...) { ...; return this; }` and java.util.stream pipelines with one terminal operation
implementation_notes: Java writes the mutable chain by hand - each step returns this and the terminal build() returns the product, the shape Bloch's builder documents - and the JDK also ships the pattern as an API style: java.util.stream chains lazy intermediate operations (filter, map, sorted) and ends at exactly one terminal operation (collect, forEach, reduce), while StringBuilder.append returns the builder. Java has no extension methods and no this.type, so the fluent surface must live on the class itself (or on a dedicated builder), and inherited chains return the base type unless each step is overridden with a covariant return type (Java 5+). Prefer the immutable pipeline shape when chains are stored or shared, the mutable receiver-returning builder when one thread assembles one object.
pitfalls: A Stream is consumed by its terminal operation: keeping a Stream in a field and reusing it in a second chain throws IllegalStateException - store a factory or the source collection, not the pipeline.
Adding DSL verbs (`with`, `skippable`) to a domain class breaks its command-query API and exposes intermediate invalid states; put the fluent surface on a builder or expression builder.
Checked exceptions do not fit a chain: a failing step must throw unchecked, defer to a throwing terminal method, or smuggle the failure, and in the last case the compiler offers no help.
